reason: While the text does depict a conflict between two peoples—the Israelites (בְנֵֽי־ יִשְׂרָאֵל) and the Egyptians (מִצְרַיִם)—on a national/collective level, the religious dimension is actually central and dominant throughout the passage, not absent. The narrative is saturated with religious language and divine agency: the Israelites cry out to the LORD (אֶל־ יְהוָֽה), Moses explicitly frames the conflict as God's battle ('יְהוָ֖ה יִלָּחֵ֣ם לָכֶ֑ם' - 'the LORD will fight for you'), God's angel and cloud pillar actively intervene to separate the camps, God 'looked down' upon the Egyptian camp (וַיַּשְׁקֵ֤ף יְהוָה), and the passage concludes with the Israelites fearing and believing in the LORD. The conflict is explicitly framed as God's salvation (יְשׁוּעַ֣ת יְהוָ֔ה) and God's mighty hand (הַיָּ֣ד הַגְּדֹלָ֗ה אֲשֶׁ֨ר עָשָׂ֤ה יְהוָה). The divine/religious dimension is not incidental—it is the primary interpretive framework through which the national conflict is understood.
